home.title: Understanding the Bible in context
home.intro: I’m building this site as a window into biblical scholarship. I want people to be able to read related passages side by side and get a better sense of what scholars are saying about them, with sources they can follow.
home.note: You don’t need a background in biblical studies to get started.
home.exploreIntro: The Gospel comparison is ready to read. The Torah sections describe what’s planned.
home.welcomeText: Christians, people from other faiths, and people who aren’t religious are all welcome. I want the explanations to be useful whatever your starting point. You can read more about how I’m choosing sources and handling disagreements on the methods page.

about.title: About this project
about.intro: I want to build a place where people can get into biblical scholarship without needing to have studied it first. Comparing passages is one way to start.

paragraphs.text: This site is for anyone who wants to understand the Bible better. Christians, readers from other religious traditions, and people with no religious affiliation are welcome. You don’t need specialist training or a particular view of the Bible to use it.

The focus here is on historical and literary questions: how a passage is written, how it relates to other texts, and what we can say about its setting. Dale B. Martin explains how this differs from theological reading. Readers may find both approaches useful.

I want to explain the arguments fairly and show what supports them. Scholars disagree, and those disagreements are part of the subject. Where one explanation has stronger evidence than another, that should be made clear too.

definitions.text: The biblical passages themselves, with their references and translation identified.
The reading prompts, passage groupings, and observations written for this site. Direct observations point back to the passages you can inspect.
Attributed arguments supported by academic sources. A hypothesis is a proposed explanation, not a label we treat as an established fact.

paragraphs.text: Explanations will cite scholarly books, peer-reviewed research, academic reference works, or official academic institutions. References include a page, section, or timestamp when it can be checked. When scholars disagree, the explanation should say whose view it presents.
For the future Torah sources tool, an assignment to a hypothetical source will always name the scholarly model it belongs to. It won’t appear as an agreed fact about the verse.
The comparison uses the Berean Standard Bible (BSB), provided by AO Lab’s Free Use Bible API. That service supplies the Bible text. Historical and interpretive claims have separate academic sources.

link.label: The publisher places the text in the public domain.

paragraphs.text: Verse numbers, paragraph breaks, poetry, and translator notes are kept where the provider supplies them. English wording is useful for reading a translation, but it isn’t enough to establish a relationship between Greek or Hebrew texts.
If a passage doesn’t load, you’ll see an error and a retry button. The site won’t switch to another translation. Adding a translation will depend on its availability and licensing.
There’s one Gospel comparison to read and three pages outlining the planned tools. You don’t need an account. Saved reading progress hasn’t been added.

comparison.intro: Matthew 8:23–27, Mark 4:35–41, and Luke 8:22–25. Read the accounts together, or switch to whole passages to follow each one on its own.
comparison.help: The groups below connect related parts of the story. They aren’t word-for-word alignments. Each account stays in its original verse order.
comparison.caution: English wording helps us compare this translation. It cannot, on its own, establish relationships between the Greek texts or prove a particular source theory.

synoptic.title: What does “Synoptic” mean?
synoptic.text: Here, “Synoptic” is a convenient label for reading Matthew, Mark, and Luke together. You can compare the accounts without first choosing a theory about their relationship.

other.title: How the explanations will be sourced
other.text: The notes will distinguish observations about a passage from a scholar’s interpretation. Each substantive claim will point to a source you can check.
